 WTA Tokyo Quarterfinal Predictions Including Elena Rybakina vs Leylah Fernandez 
 Share Share this article
 × X Facebook LinkedIn WhatsApp Reddit Email Copy 
 The WTA Tokyo quarterfinals are set and it promises to be an entertaining day of tennis in the Japanese capital. As always, we here at LWOT will be offering our predictions for every match on the slate, including a repeat of last week’s Ningbo final, as well as all the action in Guangzhou . Who will make it to the last four in Tokyo?
 WTA Tokyo Quarterfinal Predictions
 Kamilla Rakhimova vs Maya Joint
 Head-to-head: first meeting
 Kamilla Rakhimova has the ranking edge, sitting 28 places above Maya Joint at world #66, and she has just shown her nerve by outlasting Ekaterina Alexandrova in a decider tie-break. That kind of win breeds belief. But Joint is no pushover. The Aussie has been one of the week’s stories, and she bounced back from a lopsided second set against Cristina Bucsa to close it out. This is their first meeting, so neither player has a blueprint.
 Expect a scrap. Both are coming off three-setters, both have momentum, and neither is likely to blink early, so a long afternoon with plenty of games is on the horizon. Rakhimova’s composure under pressure gives her a narrow edge, but if Joint’s confidence and the home-style support keep flowing, she wins this one at WTA Tokyo.
 Prediction: Joint in 3 
 Diana Shnaider vs Alexandra Eala
 Head-to-head: first meeting
 Diana Shnaider arrives in the Tokyo quarterfinals with momentum and a point to prove. The WTA Tokyo third seed shrugged off a mid-match wobble against Aliaksandra Sasnovich, closing out a 6-3 5-7 6-3 win, and she holds the one thing that matters in a rematch: a recent win over her opponent. Her left-handed, heavy-hitting baseline game has been too much for Alexandra Eala before, and the 7-5 6-4 result in Ningbo last week suggests the template still works.
 Eala, though, will not go quietly. The eighth seed roared back from a set down to dispatch Talia Gibson 4-6 6-2 6-0, and that kind of finish breeds belief. A quick-fire revenge mission is a tempting storyline, and the Ningbo scoreline showed how narrow the gap can be. Still, we like Shnaider in this match-up on this surface.
 Prediction: Shnaider in 3 
 Jan 17, 2025; Melbourne, Victoria, Australia; Diana Shnaider hits a forehand during her match against Donna Vekic of Croatia in the third round of the women’s singles at the 2025 Australian Open at Melbourne Park. Mandatory Credit: Mike Frey-Imagn Images 
 Alycia Parks vs Mia Pohankova
 Head-to-head: first meeting
 Alycia Parks has the bigger weapons, and in a Tokyo quarterfinal on a quick hard court it should count for plenty. Her serve is built for these conditions: it skids, it jumps, and when it lands, points end before Pohankova can settle. The risk is that Parks can be her own worst enemy. Double faults arrive in clusters, and a quarterfinal is a bad time to hand out free games. Win the first-serve battle, and she’s through quickly. Lose it, and the match turns into a scrap.
 That scrap is Pohankova’s best route. The young Slovak has already shown a knack for upsetting seeded players this week at WTA Toyko, and she’ll look to turn this into a rally contest: take the pace, attack the second serve, and make Parks play one ball too many. If the nerves creep into the American’s toss, the upset is on. But power plus experience usually wins at this stage.
 Prediction: Parks in 3 
 Elena Rybakina vs Leylah Fernandez
 Head-to-head: Rybakina 4-2 Fernandez
 Elena Rybakina meets Leylah Fernandez in the quarterfinals, a replay of the Ningbo final, and the world #1 arrives with nothing left to prove and plenty left to take. She clinched the year-end top ranking with a 6-2, 6-3 win over Yulia Putintseva, a tidy 70-minute job that left her fresh.
 Fernandez, by contrast, had to grind past Elise Mertens 6-2, 7-6(8) to get here, and the tiebreak-sized scare says she’s running on guts as much as gas. The Canadian’s lefty spin and flat-footed-opponent angles are real problems, but Rybakina’s serve and first-strike forehand tend to shorten the questions before they’re asked.
 Ningbo was only days ago, so no secrets remain. Rybakina knows what’s coming, and the title-holder has the psychological edge in that final. Fernandez’s route to an upset runs through long, ugly rallies and one early break she can hold onto. Without that, this is a coronation lap for the year-end #1.
 Prediction: Rybakina in 2
